p1.t: Be honest, Lama. What do you think of my Reading Week poster? I'd really like some constructive criticism.

dialogue.scene: Emma and Fahad are reading an article about teenagers and sleep before a class discussion.

p1.t: This article says teenagers are lazy because they sleep until noon. That's a sweeping generalisation, isn't it?
Definitely. It comes across as a bit unfair. Teenagers tend to sleep later, but there's a scientific reason for it.
Right. Our body clocks seem to shift as we grow up, so we don't feel sleepy until later at night.
That's true to some extent. But lots of us also stay up late chatting with friends.

p2.t: So, on the whole, would you say our class is sleep-deprived?
Quite a few of us appear to be, especially during exam week. Not everyone, though.
Then schools that start a bit later might actually help students concentrate.
Possibly. It seems that some schools abroad have tried it, with fairly good results.

dialogue.scene: After a family lunch in the majlis, Reem's grandfather tells her what he thinks she should study at university.

p1.t: Reem, your uncle is a doctor, and so was my father. You'd make an excellent doctor too.
Thank you, Grandad. I can see where you're coming from, but I've set my heart on architecture.
Architecture? Doctors help people every day. It's a far more useful job.
With all due respect, I'm not entirely convinced that's true. Architects seem to help people in a different way.

p2.t: How so?
Well, good buildings tend to make people healthier and happier. Think of hospitals with lots of natural light.
Hmm. I suppose I hadn't looked at it like that.

dialogue.scene: Dana and Hessa present 'Ask Dana', the advice slot on their school radio. Today a student has sent in a tricky problem.

p1.t: Welcome back! Today's message says: 'My best friend wants to read her very long poem on National Day. What should I tell her?'

Exactly. You need to strike a balance. Start with what you genuinely like about the poem.
Then you could perhaps say: 'It seems a little long for a short event. I wonder if you could choose your best verses?'

p2.t: That's tactful. It doesn't come across as criticism; it sounds like advice.
And she still gets to perform, which is what really matters to her.
So, to our listener: be kind, but be clear. That's how you get your message across.

dialogue.scene: Reem is chairing a panel on the school radio. The question is whether volunteering should be compulsory for students.

p1.t: Welcome to our panel. Today's question: should volunteering be compulsory for students? Dana, you have the floor. Please keep it brief.
Thanks. I think it should stay voluntary. If people are forced, they won't really care about the work.
Sorry to interrupt, but isn't that true of homework too? We still have to do it.
If I could just finish, homework is for our own learning, but volunteering should come from the heart.

p2.t: You both make a valid point. Lama, would you like to say more?
Yes. Going back to Dana's point, many students never try volunteering simply because nobody asks them. A few required hours could change that.
That's fair. Maybe a few hours, but students should choose the activity themselves.
So, a compromise! Let's wrap up there. Chairing this discussion was easier than I thought. Thank you both!

dialogue.focus: Sorry to interrupt, but isn't that true of homework too?

dialogue.scene: Omar is interviewing his cousin Majid, a young Arabic calligrapher, for the school magazine.

p1.t: So, Majid, when did you take up calligraphy?
About three years ago. My grandfather showed me some Thuluth script, and I was hooked.
You're clearly passionate about it. What do you love about it most?
What I love about calligraphy is the patience it needs. One wrong move and you have to start again.

p2.t: That sounds stressful! Don't take this the wrong way, but isn't it a bit boring?
Not at all. Actually, it's therapeutic. When I'm writing, I lose track of time completely.
And what makes it special compared with other kinds of art?

Some Saudi start-ups, such as the delivery app Jahez, have grown into large companies.
Programmes in Riyadh and other cities help young people turn ideas into businesses.
qs: Which app do you think people in Saudi Arabia still need?
What makes a new app catch on?

3-0.exit: Judge an app you use every day: give its main strength and its main drawback.

3-1.objective: Today you will compare and judge different solutions to traffic problems near schools.
3-1.warmup: What is the traffic like near your school in the morning?

expressions.frame: ___ is nowhere near as ___ as …

dialogue.scene: Saad and Majid from the student council are judging ideas to reduce the traffic jam outside their school every morning.

p1.t: OK, we've got three ideas to tackle the morning traffic: a school bus, staggered start times and a weekly 'walk to school' day.
The bus is the best option in the long term. It would take dozens of cars off the road.
True. It's questionable whether enough families would pay for it, though.
Fair enough. What about staggered start times? Younger classes could start fifteen minutes earlier.

p2.t: On paper, it's simple. But is it feasible? Parents with children in different years would have to come twice.
Good point. And the walking day?
It's nice, but it's only a short-term fix. One day a week is nowhere near as effective as a daily bus.
So the bus is still our strongest option. The main drawback is cost, so let's ask the school about a discount.

dialogue.focus: It's questionable whether enough families would pay for it, though.
qs: Which three ideas do Saad and Majid discuss?
Why might staggered start times not be feasible?

speakout.scene: Your town council wants ideas to reduce traffic near schools. You are judging three ideas: a school bus, a car-free zone near the gate, and online classes once a week.

prompts.q: What do you think of the school bus idea?
prompts.hint: Judge it 'in the long term' and mention one drawback.

prompts.q: And the car-free zone?
prompts.hint: Say whether it's feasible, using 'It's questionable whether …'.

prompts.q: Which idea is the weakest?
prompts.hint: Compare with 'nowhere near as … as' or call it 'only a short-term fix'.

culture.title: Around the world: School Streets
points: In some UK cities, roads outside schools are closed to cars at the start and end of the school day.
These 'School Streets' aim to cut pollution and make walking and cycling safer.
Some studies found that more children walked or cycled to school after the change.
qs: Would a 'School Street' work outside your school? Why or why not?
How do most students at your school get there?

3-1.exit: Judge two ways of getting to school, by car and by bus, using 'far more … than' and 'in the long term'.

3-2.warmup: What does your school or family do to save water or electricity?

dialogue.scene: Emma and Reem from the eco club have money for one green project at their international school in Jeddah.

p1.t: We've got a budget for one green project. Let's weigh up the two options: solar panels or water-saving taps.
Solar panels make so much sense here. We have sunshine almost every day.
True, but the upfront cost is huge. It could take years before they pay off.
In the long term, though, the benefits outweigh the costs. The school's electricity bill would drop.

p2.t: Maybe. But water-saving taps are far cheaper and much more cost-effective in the short term.
That's a fair point. Their main drawback is that students might not even notice them.
That's exactly why we'd need posters too. Water is precious in a desert country.
OK. It remains to be seen whether the head will agree, but let's present both options.

dialogue.focus: In the long term, though, the benefits outweigh the costs.
qs: What two options is the eco club considering?
Why is Emma worried about the solar panels?

speakout.scene: Your school has money for one green project: a vegetable garden, recycling bins in every classroom, or solar-powered lights for the playground. Judge the options.

prompts.q: Which option is the most cost-effective?
prompts.hint: Compare the costs, using 'cost-effective' or 'upfront cost'.

prompts.q: Would the garden really be worth the effort?
prompts.hint: Use 'In the long term, the benefits outweigh …' or 'It remains to be seen whether …'.

prompts.q: So which one would you choose?
prompts.hint: Weigh up the options and give a final judgement with a reason.

culture.title: Around Saudi Arabia: The Saudi Green Initiative
points: The Saudi Green Initiative was launched in 2021.
One of its goals is to plant ten billion trees across the country over the coming decades.
It also aims to protect land and sea areas and to increase the use of renewable energy.
qs: Which green project would you like to see in your city?
Do the benefits of planting trees in the desert outweigh the costs? Why?

3-2.exit: Judge one green idea for your home: say whether the benefits outweigh the costs, and why.

3-3.objective: Today you will give a balanced judgement on using AI tools for schoolwork.
3-3.warmup: Have you ever used an AI tool to help you learn? What did you use it for?

expressions.def: after thinking about all the facts

expressions.def: people haven't decided yet if something is good

expressions.def: something with both good and bad effects

dialogue.scene: Lama asks her older cousin Sara, a university student, what she thinks about using AI chatbots for homework.

p1.t: Some of my classmates use AI chatbots for all their essays. Is that such a bad thing?
Honestly, AI is a double-edged sword. It can explain things brilliantly, but it can also become a shortcut.
A shortcut to what?
To good marks without real learning. If you rely on it for everything, you never build critical thinking.

p2.t: But it's debatable whether teachers can even tell the difference.
Maybe not, but you'll notice the difference in your exams, when there's no chatbot to help.
Fair enough. So should students avoid it completely?
Not at all. The jury is still out, but on balance, I'd use it as a tutor, not a writer.

dialogue.focus: Honestly, AI is a double-edged sword.
qs: Why does Sara call AI a double-edged sword?
How does Sara think students should use AI?

speakout.scene: Your school is deciding whether to allow AI tools in class. You are on the student panel and must judge the idea.

prompts.q: What's the biggest advantage of allowing AI in class?
prompts.hint: Give one clear advantage and an example.

prompts.q: And the biggest risk?
prompts.hint: Use 'a double-edged sword' or 'The main drawback is …'.

prompts.q: So, on balance, should the school allow it?
prompts.hint: Start with 'On balance, …' and add a condition.

culture.title: Around the world: AI in the Classroom
points: Schools around the world are trying to decide how students should use AI tools.
Some schools ban them for homework, while others teach students to use them responsibly.
Many teachers now ask students to explain their thinking aloud, which AI cannot do for them.
qs: Should students be taught how to use AI at school? Why?
Which school skills will still matter most in a world with AI?

3-3.exit: Give a balanced judgement, in two sentences, on using calculators in maths lessons.

dialogue.scene: Turki and Sam, the class representatives, must decide how to spend the money left in the class fund.

p1.t: We've got 3,000 riyals left in the class fund. We need to narrow down the ideas to one.
Let's rule out the new football kit. Only half the class plays football, so it's hard to justify.
Agreed. That leaves the trip to the science centre and the class party.
The party would be fun, but it's over in three hours. The trip is by far the best value for money.

p2.t: True. We'd learn something and still have fun. The main drawback is transport.
The school bus is free if we book early, so that's not really a problem.
Perfect. Then the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks. Let's go for the trip.
Great. I'm sure it'll be worth every riyal.

dialogue.focus: The trip is by far the best value for money.
qs: Why do they rule out the football kit?
Why does Sam prefer the trip to the party?

speakout.scene: Your family has 2,000 riyals to spend on something for everyone: a weekend trip, a new TV, or a family membership at a sports club. Help them decide.

prompts.q: Which option would you rule out first, and why?
prompts.hint: Use 'I'd rule out … because …'.

prompts.q: Which option is the best value for money?

culture.title: Around the world: Learning to Budget
points: In many countries, teenagers receive a regular allowance so that they can practise managing money.
Many experts suggest a simple rule: save part of your money before you spend the rest.
Comparing prices and asking 'Do I really need this?' helps people avoid wasting money.
qs: Do you save part of your money? Why or why not?
Should schools teach students how to manage money? Why?

3-4.exit: Judge something you bought recently: was it good value for money? Explain why.

dialogue.scene: Hamad and Leo are judges at their school's Innovation Challenge. Three teams have presented their projects.

p1.t: Right, let's judge the three projects against our criteria: originality, cost and how practical they are.
The drone that delivers books between classrooms is original, but it seems a bit far-fetched.
I agree. It's debatable whether it would be safe in crowded corridors.
The smart water bottle is clever, but the main drawback is the price. Each one costs 200 riyals.

p2.t: So that leaves the app for reporting broken things around the school.
It's simple, but it stands up to scrutiny. It's cheap, practical and easy to use.
Then it's by far the strongest project. Are we ready to reach a verdict?
Yes. The app comes out on top. Let's announce it!

dialogue.focus: It's debatable whether it would be safe in crowded corridors.
qs: What are the judges' three criteria?
Why do the judges choose the app?

speakout.scene: You are a judge at your school's Innovation Challenge. The teams have presented a solar-powered bench that charges phones, a 'lost and found' app and a robot that cleans whiteboards. Judge them with your partner (the teacher).

prompts.q: What criteria should we use to judge the projects?
prompts.hint: Suggest two or three criteria and explain why they matter.

prompts.q: Which project has the biggest weakness?
prompts.hint: Use 'The main drawback is …' or 'far-fetched'.

prompts.q: So, which project comes out on top?
prompts.hint: Reach a verdict with 'by far' and give two reasons.

culture.title: Around the world: 5,127 Prototypes
points: The inventor James Dyson says he built 5,127 prototypes before his bagless vacuum cleaner worked.
Each failed version helped him find and fix a problem.
His story shows that judging your own ideas honestly is part of inventing.
qs: Would you keep going after a hundred failed attempts? Why?
What criteria would you use to judge your own ideas?

3-5.exit: Choose the best invention of the last fifty years and give your verdict, with one strength and one drawback.

words.ex: Thanks for the constructive criticism; it really helped.
The dark colours come across as rather serious.
The text is a bit on the small side.
I'm not entirely sure that the title fits the topic.
You could tone down the red a little.
Your choice of photos is spot on.

dialogue.t: Be honest, Lama. What do you think of my Reading Week poster? I'd really like some constructive criticism.
Well, the photos are spot on. The bright orange, though, comes across as a bit loud to me.
Really? I thought it would catch people's attention.
It does, but it seems to pull your eyes away from the message. You could perhaps tone it down slightly.
OK, maybe a softer orange. What about the title?
It's a bit on the small side. I'm not entirely sure that people will see it from the back of the hall.

grammar.title: Softening criticism
grammar.ar: نخفّف النقد بكلمات مثل a bit / slightly / a little وبعبارات مثل It seems … و I'm not entirely sure that …

I'm not entirely sure that the ending works.

words.ex: Teenagers tend to go to bed later than adults.
On the whole, our class gets too little sleep.
I agree with you to some extent, but not completely.
'All teenagers are lazy' is a sweeping generalisation.
Many students are sleep-deprived during exam week.
I stayed up late to finish my science project.

dialogue.t: This article says teenagers are lazy because they sleep until noon. That's a sweeping generalisation, isn't it?
Definitely. It comes across as a bit unfair. Teenagers tend to sleep later, but there's a scientific reason for it.
Right. Our body clocks seem to shift as we grow up, so we don't feel sleepy until later at night.
That's true to some extent. But lots of us also stay up late chatting with friends.
So, on the whole, would you say our class is sleep-deprived?
Quite a few of us appear to be, especially during exam week. Not everyone, though.

grammar.title: tend to and seem to

dialogue.t: Reem, your uncle is a doctor, and so was my father. You'd make an excellent doctor too.
Thank you, Grandad. I can see where you're coming from, but I've set my heart on architecture.
Architecture? Doctors help people every day. It's a far more useful job.
With all due respect, I'm not entirely convinced that's true. Architects seem to help people in a different way.
How so?
Well, good buildings tend to make people healthier and happier. Think of hospitals with lots of natural light.

Come on, it'll only take five minutes!
I know, but if Mr Ali noticed, we'd both be in a tricky position. It seems a bit risky to me.
Fair enough. I just don't understand question four at all.
Well, I'm happy to lend a hand with that. Shall we go through it together at break?

grammar.title: Declining politely

I'd rather not, if that's OK.
I can't this weekend, but how about next Thursday?

Sure. Is everything OK?
Well, this is a bit awkward, but it seems that we've fallen behind with the slides, and the deadline is on Thursday.
Ah. Yes, I haven't started my part yet. I've had football training every evening.
I understand. But I'm not entirely sure that Omar and I can finish everything alone. I wonder if you could do your slides by Tuesday.
That's fair. I know I haven't been pulling my weight lately.

grammar.title: Raising a problem politely

It seems that some of the work hasn't been done.
I wonder if you could finish your part by Tuesday.

words.ex: It was very tactful of you not to mention her mistake.
My brother is so blunt that he sometimes upsets people.
I didn't mean to hurt your feelings.
Stop beating around the bush and tell me.
You need to strike a balance between honesty and kindness.
A short example helps you get your message across.

dialogue.t: Welcome back! Today's message says: 'My best friend wants to read her very long poem on National Day. What should I tell her?'
Tricky! If you're too blunt, you might hurt her feelings. But if you beat around the bush, she won't understand.
Exactly. You need to strike a balance. Start with what you genuinely like about the poem.
Then you could perhaps say: 'It seems a little long for a short event. I wonder if you could choose your best verses?'
So, to our listener: be kind, but be clear. That's how you get your message across.
Keep your messages coming, everyone. See you next week!

Sorry to interrupt, but who's bringing the tent? Last time we forgot it.
Good point. My uncle has a big one. Anyway, after dinner we'll—
Can I just add something? The weather app says it might get really cold after midnight.
Ah. OK, so everyone needs warm blankets. As I was saying, after dinner we'll watch the stars.
Could I come in here? Last time we all talked over each other and nobody decided anything.
True! Let's take turns this time. I'll chip in with snacks and my telescope.

Taif again? We went there last year!
Hold on a second, Yousef. If I could just finish, I've got two other ideas too.
Go on, Lama. Bear with her, Yousef.
Thanks. As I was saying, Taif is cooler. The second option is Al-Baha, and the third is the Red Sea coast.
The Red Sea! Now you're talking. Sorry I kept interrupting.

Can I just add one more thing? We could use bean bags instead of hard chairs.

Sorry, guys, we're getting sidetracked. That's interesting, but it's a bit off the point.
Fair enough. Where were we?
Going back to what Sam said about the moon, that's a good idea. A night with no moon means darker skies.

Thanks. I think it should stay voluntary. If people are forced, they won't really care about the work.
Sorry to interrupt, but isn't that true of homework too? We still have to do it.
If I could just finish, homework is for our own learning, but volunteering should come from the heart.
You both make a valid point. Lama, would you like to say more?
Yes. Going back to Dana's point, many students never try volunteering simply because nobody asks them. A few required hours could change that.

pages.text: For three months, Yousef had spent every spare moment in his grandfather's garage, surrounded by wires, motors and half-eaten bags of sunflower seeds. His goal was simple to explain but almost impossible to achieve: he wanted to build a robot that could climb a date palm and pollinate it on its own. Every spring, the farm in Al-Ahsa hired skilled climbers to do this delicate work by hand, but there were fewer of them each year. If Yousef succeeded, his robot could enter the national youth innovation competition in Riyadh. He had already given it a name, Saqr, after the falcon that never misses its target.

His grandfather, Abu Khalid, was less impressed. He had climbed palms for over fifty years with nothing but a thick rope belt called a karr and his own bare feet. "A machine cannot feel the tree," he said one evening, sipping his cardamom coffee. "The bark changes from palm to palm, and a good climber reads it like a book." Yousef bit his tongue, because arguing with his grandfather was like arguing with the wind. Instead, he promised himself that Saqr would prove him wrong.

The first real test took place on a still, golden morning in March. Saqr wrapped its metal arms around the trunk, and for a few glorious seconds it moved upwards exactly as Yousef had planned. Then, about two metres up, its grip slipped on a patch of rough, uneven bark. The robot slid down the trunk with a horrible scraping sound and landed in the sand with one arm bent at an impossible angle. Yousef stared at it, feeling as if all his hard work had been thrown away in an instant.

That night, he couldn't sleep, so he scrolled through videos of climbing robots from around the world. Most of them had been designed for smooth poles or modern buildings, not for the twisted, scaly trunk of a date palm. The competition deadline was only three weeks away, and he was running out of ideas as quickly as he was running out of time. "Back to the drawing board," he muttered, although he wasn't sure he even had a drawing board left. Eventually, he fell asleep with his phone still glowing on his chest.

When he walked into the garage the next morning, he froze in surprise. His grandfather was sitting on an upturned crate, holding Saqr's damaged arm and studying it under a torch. Beside him lay his old karr, its rope worn smooth by decades of use. "Your machine holds the tree like a frightened child," Abu Khalid said without looking up. "It squeezes too hard in the wrong places, and not at all where it matters."

Over the next hour, the old man explained something Yousef had never noticed. A skilled climber doesn't grip the trunk with constant force; he leans back into the belt, letting it tighten and loosen with each movement. The tension shifts like a heartbeat, adjusting to every bump in the bark. Yousef's eyes widened as the idea took shape in his mind. If Saqr used a flexible strap with pressure sensors, it could copy exactly what his grandfather's body had been doing for half a century.

The following weeks were a blur of late nights, burnt fingertips and countless cups of tea. Abu Khalid, who claimed he understood nothing about computers, turned up in the garage every evening with suggestions about angles and balance. He even climbed a young palm one afternoon so that Yousef could film the way his weight moved. Little by little, the new strap system began to work, and Saqr climbed higher with each test. By the end, the robot was reaching the crown of the tree, where the date flowers grew, without a single slip.

In Riyadh, the judges watched in silence as Saqr climbed a real palm trunk that had been set up in the exhibition hall. When it reached the top and gently released the pollen, the audience broke into applause. One judge asked Yousef how he had solved a problem that engineers in many countries had struggled with. Yousef glanced at the front row, where his grandfather sat in his best thobe, trying not to look proud. "I didn't solve it alone," he said. "I learned it from the best climber in Al-Ahsa."

Saqr won second place, along with a grant to develop the design further. Back at the farm, Yousef added a small engraved plate to the robot's strap that read "The Abu Khalid Grip." His grandfather pretended to find it silly, but Yousef noticed him running his fingers over the letters when he thought no one was watching. That spring, the old man and the robot worked side by side among the palms, one with rope and the other with sensors. "Perhaps a machine can feel the tree after all," Abu Khalid admitted, "as long as someone teaches it how."

pages.text: Yusuf had never imagined that a man could measure the whole world without leaving his own neighbourhood. Yet that was exactly what his teacher, the great scholar Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, intended to do. It was the early eleventh century, and they were living in the fort of Nandana, high above a wide, dusty plain in what is now Pakistan. Most of the soldiers at the fort thought the old man was slightly eccentric, because he spent his nights staring at the stars instead of sleeping. Yusuf, who was fifteen and had been his apprentice for two years, was beginning to suspect they were wrong.

One morning al-Biruni called him into his small room, which was crowded with scrolls, maps and strange brass instruments. "Bring the astrolabe," he said, "and please try not to drop it this time." Yusuf blushed, remembering the incident the week before, and carefully lifted the heavy brass disc. "Today," his teacher announced, "we are going to find out how big the Earth is." Yusuf frowned and said, "But surely the scholars in Baghdad did that long ago, didn't they?" "They did," al-Biruni replied, "but the caliph's men needed weeks in the desert with ropes and camels, whereas I intend to do it in a single afternoon, from the top of a mountain."

Before they could climb anything, however, they had to work out exactly how high the mountain was. All morning, Yusuf counted his steps across the burning plain while his teacher measured the angle to the summit from two different points. By midday, sweat was running into Yusuf's eyes and his patience was wearing thin. "Teacher, couldn't we just guess the height?" he asked, wiping his face with his sleeve. Al-Biruni gave him a look that was half amused and half disappointed. "A guess is only a wish dressed up as knowledge," he said, "so let us measure it again, just to be certain."

In the afternoon they began the climb, following a narrow goat path that twisted up the rocky slope. Halfway up, a loose stone rolled beneath Yusuf's foot and he lost his balance. For one terrible moment the astrolabe slipped from his grip, and his heart was in his mouth as it slid towards the edge. Throwing himself forward, he caught it just before it disappeared into the valley below. When he finally stood up, trembling, al-Biruni simply nodded and said, "Good. Now you understand why I asked you not to drop it."

By the time they reached the summit, a thick yellow haze had drifted across the plain. The horizon, which should have been a sharp line, had vanished into a blur of dust and cloud. Yusuf's heart sank, because he realised that if the haze did not clear, the whole exhausting day would have been wasted. His teacher, however, did not seem worried at all; he calmly laid out his prayer mat, prayed Asr, and then sat down on a rock to wait. "The sky does not hurry for anyone," he murmured, "not even for scientists."

Then, just as the sun began to lower, a cool wind swept up from the valley and blew the haze away. Suddenly the horizon appeared again, a perfect line where the earth met the sky, stretching for miles in every direction. "Quickly, Yusuf, hold it steady!" al-Biruni called, raising the astrolabe to his eye. He was measuring something so tiny that Yusuf could hardly believe it mattered: how far the horizon dipped below a perfectly level line. Yusuf's hands were shaking with excitement, but his teacher's were as steady as the rock beneath them.

On the way down, Yusuf finally plucked up the courage to ask what the tiny angle actually meant. "Think about it," al-Biruni said, drawing a circle in the dust with a stick. "If the Earth were flat, the horizon would be exactly level with my eye, but because the Earth is round, it curves away and the horizon drops slightly." He drew a line from the mountaintop to the edge of the circle, forming a long, thin triangle. "Once we know the height of the mountain and the size of that angle, the triangle will tell us everything else, including the distance to the centre of the Earth."

That night, by the light of a flickering oil lamp, they worked through page after page of calculations. Yusuf read out the numbers while his teacher checked them against his tables, muttering under his breath. Long after the fort had fallen silent, al-Biruni put down his pen and leaned back with a tired smile. According to his result, the radius of the Earth was about six thousand three hundred and forty kilometres in today's units. Almost a thousand years later, modern scientists using satellites would discover that he had been wrong by less than one percent.

Yusuf stepped outside into the cool night air, his head buzzing with numbers. A sleepy guard on the wall asked him what on earth the two of them had been doing all day. "We measured the world," Yusuf replied simply. The guard burst out laughing, clearly convinced that the apprentice had become as eccentric as his master. Yusuf did not mind in the least; he looked up at the stars, which no longer seemed quite so far away, and smiled to himself. For the first time, he understood that knowledge was not something you were given, but something you had to climb towards, one careful step at a time.

pages.text: For as long as Faisal could remember, the oud had been sitting on top of his grandmother's wardrobe, wrapped in a faded green cloth like a secret nobody wanted to tell. Nobody ever mentioned it, and somehow he had always known not to ask. It was the summer he turned fifteen, during a heatwave that kept everyone in Jeddah indoors, that his curiosity finally got the better of him. While his grandmother was taking her afternoon nap, he dragged a chair across the room and lifted the instrument down. When he pulled back the cloth, he saw a long crack running across its round wooden body, and a small leather notebook slipped out and landed at his feet.

The notebook was full of strange symbols: rows of numbers and Arabic letters that didn't look anything like the music Faisal had studied at school. He was still trying to make sense of them when he heard footsteps behind him. His grandmother, Noura, stood frozen in the doorway, her eyes fixed on the oud in his hands. "Your grandfather was writing something for me," she said quietly, after a long silence. "He worked on it for months, but he never got the chance to finish it." Faisal turned to the last page and saw that the lines of numbers simply stopped halfway down, followed by nothing but empty paper.

Faisal had never met his grandfather, Salem, who had been a fisherman with a famously loud laugh and, apparently, a secret talent for music. The next day, he took the notebook to Mr. Hamdan, his music teacher, hoping he could crack the code. Mr. Hamdan turned the pages slowly and gave a low whistle. "This is an old way of writing music for the oud," he explained. "Each number tells you which string to play and where to put your finger." Then he scribbled an address on a scrap of paper and said, "If anyone can help you, it's Abu Yousef, the instrument maker in Al-Balad."

The workshop was hidden down a narrow alley in the old city, between tall coral-stone houses with carved wooden balconies. Inside, the air smelled of sawdust and polish, and half-built instruments hung from the ceiling like sleeping bats. Abu Yousef, a small man with thick glasses, took one look at the oud and let out a delighted laugh. "I'd know this anywhere, because I made it myself, back in 1979!" he exclaimed. "Salem couldn't afford to pay me all at once, so he brought me fresh fish every Friday for six months."

Abu Yousef agreed to repair the oud on one condition: Faisal had to help with every step. For the next three weeks, Faisal spent his afternoons sanding thin strips of wood, mixing glue and learning that rushing a job only meant doing it twice. Meanwhile, the old man taught him to read the notebook, explaining that the melody was written in maqam Bayati, a scale that could sound both joyful and heartbreaking at the same time. Little by little, the strange numbers began to turn into music under Faisal's fingers. For the first time, he felt as if he were having a conversation with a man he had never met.

There was just one problem: the song still had no ending. Faisal tried dozens of possibilities, staying up late and recording himself on his phone, but every ending he invented sounded wrong, like wearing someone else's shoes. One evening, completely fed up, he pushed the notebook away and told Abu Yousef that he was ready to give up. The old man didn't argue; he simply polished his glasses and said, "Your grandfather didn't leave the ending in the notebook, my son. Perhaps he left it somewhere else." Faisal walked home that night turning those words over and over in his mind.

Instead of searching for notes, Faisal decided to search for memories, so he asked his grandmother to tell him about Salem. She talked for hours, about his terrible jokes, his patience with his nets and the way he always came home smelling of salt and sea. "Every evening, he would sit on our balcony facing the water and hum the same little tune," she said with a smile. "I teased him about it for forty years." Faisal asked her to hum it, and when she did, a little unsure at first, he suddenly realised that it fitted the last line of the notebook perfectly. The ending had been in her memory all along.

The repaired oud was ready just in time for Eid. That evening, the whole family gathered in his grandparents' living room, the smell of cardamom coffee and sweet maamoul filling the air. Faisal's hands were shaking as he tuned the strings, and for a terrible moment he thought he would forget everything. Then he began to play, and the melody rose and fell like waves, joyful and heartbreaking at the same time, exactly as Abu Yousef had promised. When he reached the final line, his grandmother's tune, she closed her eyes and the room went completely silent.

For a moment nobody moved, and then his grandmother reached over and squeezed his hand. "Now it's finished," she whispered, her eyes shining with tears. Later that night, Faisal opened the leather notebook to the first blank page and, after a moment's hesitation, began writing a melody of his own. At the top of the page, in careful letters, he wrote: For Salem, from the grandson you never met. The oud no longer sits on top of the wardrobe; instead, it hangs on the living room wall, where anyone can take it down and play.

pages.text: Every summer, fifteen-year-old Yousef worked in his grandfather's perfume shop in Al-Balad, the old heart of Jeddah, where coral-stone houses leaned over narrow lanes. The shop was tiny and dark, but it held the most precious thing his family owned: a square glass bottle of oud oil called Layali. It had been aged for forty years, and his grandfather refused to sell it, no matter how much he was offered. Yousef had smelled it only once, as a small boy, and the memory had never left him. It was deep and smoky, like a winter night in the desert.

One Thursday morning, a wealthy collector from Dubai arrived, hoping to persuade the old man to change his mind. Grandfather smiled politely, unlocked the glass cabinet and carefully removed the wax seal from Layali. The moment the bottle was opened, Yousef frowned. The scent was thin and sweet, with a cheap note of jasmine that had no business being there. "Grandfather," he whispered, "that isn't Layali." The old man raised the bottle to his nose, and his face turned as pale as paper.

After the embarrassed collector had left, Grandfather sank into his chair as if he had aged ten years in ten minutes. "Only two people have keys to that cabinet," he said quietly. "Me, and Saleem, who has kept my accounts for twenty years and is on holiday in Abha." That left Hamza, the shy assistant who had started working there a month earlier, as the obvious suspect. Grandfather wanted to avoid a scandal, so Yousef begged him to wait one day before calling the police. Reluctantly, the old man agreed.

Yousef soon noticed that Hamza seemed jumpy, avoiding his eyes whenever he spoke to him. Behind some boxes in the storeroom, Yousef discovered a folded blanket, a pillow and a phone charger. When he asked about them, Hamza's voice shook as he admitted he had lost his room and had been secretly sleeping in the shop. "On Tuesday night, I saw a light and heard someone at the cabinet," he confessed. "I assumed it was your grandfather, and I was too ashamed to come out."

That evening, Yousef smelled the fake oil again, and suddenly he remembered where he had come across that sugary jasmine before. It was a blend sold by Abu Nasser, who ran a cheerful little stall at the edge of the souq. Yousef went straight there and described the bottle. "Ah, yes," said Abu Nasser, stroking his beard. "On Tuesday morning, a man in sunglasses bought exactly that amount and asked me to make it as dark as possible."

The next morning, Saleem returned, looking relaxed and carrying a leather bag. He listened to the news with a shocked expression and shook his head sadly. "It must have been the new boy," he said gently. "You can never really know a stranger." While he was talking, Yousef glanced at the shop's ledger, and his heart skipped a beat: there was an entry dated Tuesday evening, written in Saleem's famous green ink.

Yousef took a deep breath and tried to keep his voice steady. "Uncle Saleem, you said you were in Abha all week, yet you wrote in the ledger on Tuesday," he began. "That same night, someone was seen at the cabinet, and that morning a man in sunglasses bought fake oil identical to what we found." Saleem laughed nervously and claimed he must have written the wrong date. Then Yousef leaned closer and said softly, "There's one more thing. Your bag smells of Layali."

For a long moment, nobody spoke, and then Saleem's shoulders dropped. With tears in his eyes, he explained that his own business had collapsed and he was drowning in debts he had been too proud to mention. He had planned to sell the oil abroad, but he had not yet found a buyer. Slowly, he opened his bag and placed the real Layali on the counter. "I have known you for twenty years," Grandfather said, his voice heavy with disappointment, "and you never once asked me for help."

Saleem left the shop that day for good, but Grandfather promised to help him find an honest way to repay his debts. Hamza was given a small room above the shop, and a proper salary to go with it. That night, Grandfather poured a single drop of Layali onto Yousef's wrist. "A good nose found the truth," he said, "but a good heart decided what to do with it." Yousef breathed in the deep, smoky scent and smiled, knowing he would never forget this summer.

pages.text: It started on a perfectly ordinary Tuesday, in the middle of a maths test that Faisal was quietly failing. At exactly 10:17, the school bell rang for one long minute, then fell silent. Thirty heads lifted at once, and Mr. Hamdan frowned at the clock as if it had personally insulted him. Break wasn't until 10:45, so nobody moved, but the whisper spread around the room like wildfire.

By the end of the week, the bell had rung at 10:17 every single day, and the rumours were getting wilder. Some boys claimed the school was haunted, while others insisted it was a secret fire drill. Faisal, who edited the school newsletter with his best friend Majed, saw an opportunity. "This is the story we've been waiting for," he said, tapping his notebook. "If we find out who's behind it, everyone will finally read what we write."

Faisal already had a suspect in mind: Tariq, a quiet boy from the year above who was famous for building robots and fixing anything with a screen. "He's been seen near the admin office twice this week," Faisal said. "It has to be him." Majed looked sceptical. "Seen by whom? You can't just jump to conclusions because someone is good with computers." But Faisal had already started scribbling a headline: Tech Genius Behind Bell Mystery?

To gather evidence, the boys stayed behind after school and went looking for Abu Nasser, the caretaker who had worked there for over thirty years. They found him in a dusty storeroom, sorting through boxes of old trophies and faded photographs. When Faisal asked about the bell, the old man's hands stopped moving. "So it's ringing again," he murmured, almost to himself. "I never thought I'd hear that sound one more time."

Abu Nasser pulled out a black-and-white photograph of a tall man standing proudly in front of the school gates. "This was Ustadh Ibrahim, our very first headmaster," he explained. "Every day at 10:17, he rang the bell for one minute so that students and teachers could stop, breathe, and think about something they were grateful for." The tradition had faded away after he retired, and eventually the old bell system had been switched off and forgotten. "Why 10:17?" Majed asked. "Because that was the exact minute the doors first opened," the caretaker replied with a smile.

The next morning, Faisal and Majed went straight to the IT department, where they were surprised to find Tariq helping the technician. Faisal felt his face turn hot as he remembered the headline in his notebook. Tariq explained that the school had recently installed a new digital system, and during the upgrade, an ancient backup file had been accidentally restored. "It's a glitch," he said, showing them the screen. "There's one line of programming from decades ago: ring at 10:17, sixty seconds, every school day."

Walking back to class, Faisal tore the page out of his notebook and crumpled it into a tight ball. "I nearly accused him in front of the whole school," he admitted, feeling thoroughly ashamed of himself. Majed shrugged kindly. "Nearly isn't the same as actually doing it. Real journalists check their facts, remember?" That afternoon, Faisal found Tariq in the corridor and apologised, and to his relief, Tariq simply laughed and asked if he could help with the article.

The three boys spent the weekend writing the true story of Ustadh Ibrahim and the forgotten minute of gratitude. Abu Nasser lent them the old photographs, and Tariq designed the layout so that it looked genuinely professional. When the newsletter came out, copies disappeared within an hour, and even the teachers were discussing it in the staffroom. By Thursday, the headmaster had called the boys into his office, and Faisal was sure they were in trouble.

Instead, the headmaster told them he had decided not to fix the glitch at all. From then on, the bell would ring at 10:17 on purpose, and the whole school would pause to remember what they were thankful for. On the first official day, Faisal watched Abu Nasser standing in the courtyard with his eyes closed and a peaceful smile on his face. Faisal had set out to catch a culprit, but he had found something far more valuable. When the minute ended, he quietly added one more thing to his list: friends who tell you the truth.

pages.text: Sultan had been dreading the weekend for weeks. While his friends in Riyadh were planning a gaming tournament, he would be stuck at his grandfather's farm near Al-Ahsa, where the Wi-Fi was so weak it was practically non-existent. "It's only two days," his mother had said, giving him the look that meant the discussion was over. Now, as the car turned onto a dusty track lined with palm trees, he slumped in his seat. He wondered how anyone could survive a whole weekend without a decent signal.

His grandfather was waiting by the gate, a hooded falcon perched calmly on his gloved fist. "Welcome, my boy," he said, kissing Sultan on the forehead. "Sahm has been impatient to meet you properly." Sultan managed a polite smile, although he privately thought the bird looked far more interested in the fields than in him. Over a dinner of rice and lamb, his grandfather told stories of hunting trips in the desert, and Sultan bit his tongue whenever he felt the urge to check his phone.

The next afternoon, his grandfather took Sahm out for exercise, and Sultan reluctantly tagged along. The sky had been clear all morning, but by the time they reached the open ground, a yellowish haze was creeping in from the west. "The wind's changing," his grandfather muttered, frowning. Before he could call the falcon back, a sudden gust whipped sand across the field, and Sahm, startled, soared upwards and vanished into the swirling dust. For a long moment, neither of them spoke.

Back at the house, his grandfather sat silently on the steps, turning the empty leather hood over and over in his hands. Sultan had never seen him look so old. "I've had him for eleven years," he said quietly. "If he isn't found before nightfall, he might not survive the cold, or the foxes." Sultan felt a lump in his throat; only that morning he had found the bird boring, and now its absence seemed to fill the whole farm.

Then, out of the blue, Sultan remembered something his uncle had mentioned. "Grandfather, doesn't Sahm wear a small tracker on his leg?" His grandfather shrugged; the device had been fitted months ago, but he had never bothered to learn how it worked. Sultan grabbed his phone, found the app his uncle had installed, and waited impatiently as the weak signal struggled to connect. At last, a tiny red dot appeared on the map, about four kilometres to the north-east.

The dot, however, wasn't moving, and the area around it appeared completely empty on the map. "That's the old village," his grandfather said slowly, his eyes widening. "Nobody has lived there for forty years. I was born in one of those houses." They set off in the pick-up truck as the storm was dying down, his grandfather driving along tracks that no app would ever show. Without the old man's knowledge, Sultan realised, finding that red dot would have been like looking for a needle in a haystack.

The village was a cluster of crumbling mud-brick houses, their wooden doors long since rotted away. The signal led them down a narrow alley to a spot where the dot seemed to sit right on top of a collapsed roof. Sultan's heart was pounding as he climbed onto a low wall, but he could see nothing except shadows and broken beams. "Be still," his grandfather whispered. Then he gave a long, low whistle that Sultan had heard him use on the farm.

For a few seconds, there was only silence. Then came a rustle of feathers, and Sahm hopped out from beneath a fallen beam, dusty but unhurt, and flew straight to the old man's outstretched glove. His grandfather laughed, and Sultan noticed that his eyes were wet. "He sheltered from the wind exactly where I used to hide from my mother when I'd been naughty," he said. "This was our house."

That evening, they sat together on the roof under the stars, with Sahm dozing on his perch nearby. His grandfather taught Sultan the whistle, patiently correcting him until the falcon finally turned its head. In return, Sultan showed him how to use the tracking app, and the old man turned out to be surprisingly quick to learn. When his mother came to collect him on Sunday, Sultan asked, much to her astonishment, whether he could come back the following weekend. "Someone has to keep an eye on Sahm," he said, grinning at his grandfather.

pages.text: Every Thursday evening, the Al-Harbi household in Riyadh smelled of cardamom and freshly baked bread, and every Thursday evening Reem sat beside her grandmother to help her with "the clever phone". Grandma Noura had been given a smartphone for her seventy-second birthday, and although she claimed it was far too complicated, she had secretly become rather attached to it. She sent voice messages to her friends, watched cooking videos and, above all, waited for calls from Faisal, Reem's older brother, who was studying engineering in Manchester. "He promised to call tonight," she said, glancing at the screen for the third time in five minutes. Reem smiled, with no idea that this particular Thursday would turn out to be anything but ordinary.

The phone rang at half past eight, and Grandma's face lit up the moment she heard the familiar voice. Within seconds, however, her smile had faded. "Grandma, I'm in trouble," the voice said, sounding breathless and frightened. "There's been an accident with my car, and the police say I have to pay for the damage tonight, or they'll keep my passport." Grandma pressed a hand to her chest, while Reem, who could hear every word on speaker, felt a cold knot form in her stomach.

"How much do you need, habibi?" Grandma asked, already reaching for the handbag where she kept her bank card. "Eight thousand riyals," the voice replied immediately. "Please send it to the account I'll text you, and please don't tell Mum and Dad, because they'll be so disappointed in me." Something about that sentence made Reem frown. Faisal had never once in his life called their parents "Mum and Dad". To him they had always been "Yumma" and "Yuba", even when he was showing off his English.

Reem leaned closer and listened more carefully, the way she listened in physics class when she suspected something would come up in the exam. The voice was undeniably Faisal's, with the same slightly husky tone and the same nervous little laugh, yet there were tiny gaps before every answer, as though someone were thinking far too hard. Even stranger, there was no background noise at all: no traffic, no wind, no police officers, nothing. She remembered an article she had read only a week earlier about criminals who used artificial intelligence to copy people's voices from short recordings online. Gently but firmly, she placed her hand over her grandmother's bank card.

"Faisal," Reem said, keeping her voice calm, "before Grandma sends anything, tell me something. When we went camping near AlUla last winter, what did you name the camel that kept trying to eat your hat?" There was a pause, longer this time, and then the voice snapped, "Reem, there's no time for silly games. I need the money now!" "It's an easy question," she insisted. The line went dead.

For a moment, neither of them spoke. Then Grandma's hands began to tremble, and Reem realised how close they had come to losing eight thousand riyals to a complete stranger. "But it was his voice," Grandma whispered. "I would know my grandson's voice anywhere." Reem hugged her and quickly called her father, who rushed in from the majlis, where he had been sitting with his cousins. Within minutes, the whole family had gathered around the phone as Reem dialled Faisal's real number on a video call.

Faisal answered from his university library, his hair messy and a pile of textbooks beside him. "What's going on? Why does everyone look as if they've seen a ghost?" he asked. When they explained, his face went pale, and then he groaned. "My videos," he said. "I've been posting short clips explaining my engineering projects, so there are hours of my voice online for anyone to use."

The next morning, Reem's father reported the call to the authorities and the bank, and he was told that scams like this had been increasing across the region. The police officer praised Reem for keeping a cool head and for asking a question that no machine could have answered from the internet. That evening, the family sat together and agreed on a secret code word that any of them would ask for if a call ever sounded suspicious. Grandma insisted on choosing it herself, and nobody was surprised when she picked the name of her favourite dish. "No robot will ever guess that," she declared proudly.

A month later, Reem stood in front of her school assembly and gave a presentation called "When Your Ears Lie to You", which her teachers later shared with families across the city. She explained how voice cloning works, why urgent requests for money should always make people suspicious, and how one simple question can protect someone you love. At the end, a girl at the back raised her hand and asked what the camel's name had actually been. Reem laughed. "Professor," she said, "because he always looked at Faisal as if he had failed every exam."

stories.title: The Madman of the Dark Room

pages.text: In the spring of 1015, the streets of Cairo were full of rumours, and most of them were about a man nobody was allowed to see. Yusuf was fifteen, the son of a palace guard, and he had never expected to become part of one of those rumours. One morning his father handed him a basket of bread, dates and lentil soup and pointed towards a narrow house near the great mosque of al-Azhar. "You'll take his meals twice a day," his father said quietly. "Don't stay long, don't ask questions, and whatever happens, don't believe a word he says."

Everyone in the city knew the story, or thought they did. The scholar Ibn al-Haytham had come from Basra after boasting that he could control the floods of the mighty Nile. The Caliph al-Hakim, a ruler famous for his sudden and terrifying moods, had sent him south to build a dam. Months later the scholar had returned empty-handed, and soon afterwards he had apparently lost his mind. When Yusuf pushed open the heavy door, he found himself in a room so dark that he could barely make out his own hands.

"Close the door behind you, please, and come and look at this," said a calm voice from the shadows. Yusuf hesitated, then did as he was told, and gradually his eyes adjusted. On the white wall opposite the shutters, a faint picture was moving: a camel, a man carrying water jars, a boy chasing a goat. Every one of them was upside down. "It's the street outside," Yusuf whispered, hardly daring to breathe. "Exactly," replied the scholar, sounding remarkably sane for a madman, "and it's coming in through that tiny hole in the shutter."

Ibn al-Haytham explained that the great Greek thinkers had believed our eyes sent out rays, like invisible fingers touching the world. "But if that were true, why can't we see in the dark?" he asked, with a gleam of amusement. "Light travels from objects to the eye, in straight lines, and this little room proves it." Yusuf frowned and pointed out that Ptolemy had been a very famous man. "So he was," the scholar agreed, "but a famous name is not evidence, and anyone who searches for the truth must be willing to doubt even his teachers."

From that day on, Yusuf's visits grew longer and longer, although he took care never to mention them at home. He began smuggling sheets of paper and pots of ink under the bread in his basket. Together they set up experiments with lamps placed at different distances, watching how the flames appeared on the wall through holes of different sizes. The scholar recorded every result with patient precision, repeating each test until he was certain. "Never trust a single result," he told Yusuf. "Test it, then test it again, and only then write it down."

One evening, heavy footsteps stopped right outside the door, and Yusuf's heart was in his mouth. An officer of the Caliph had heard that the madman was receiving far too much paper for someone who had supposedly lost his wits. Without a word, Ibn al-Haytham pushed the manuscripts towards Yusuf, who slid them beneath the empty soup pot. When the officer burst in, he found the scholar sitting on the floor, muttering nonsense to the wall and laughing at nothing. The officer shook his head in disgust and left, and Yusuf did not breathe properly again until the door had slammed shut.

"You're not mad at all, are you?" Yusuf asked once his hands had stopped trembling. The scholar was silent for a long moment before he admitted the truth. When he had stood beside the Nile at Aswan and seen the ancient temples on its banks, he had realised that if those great builders had not tamed the river, he could not either. "I could have lied to the Caliph and wasted thousands of lives on a dam that would fail," he said. "I chose to play the fool instead, because it's better to be laughed at than to deceive people who trust you."

Six long years went by, and Yusuf grew from a nervous boy into a young man with steady hands and a sharp eye. Then, in 1021, astonishing news spread through Cairo like wildfire: the Caliph had ridden out into the hills one night and had never come back. Within days, the madman of the dark room walked calmly into the sunlight, and suddenly he seemed to be perfectly well. People stared, whispered and pointed, but Ibn al-Haytham simply smiled. "Some illnesses," he remarked to Yusuf, "are cured by a change of government."

Before he set out to share his work with the scholars of the city, Ibn al-Haytham placed a thick bundle of pages into Yusuf's hands. It was a fair copy of the first chapters of his Book of Optics, and on the opening page he had written: "For Yusuf, who carried light in a basket of bread." Over the following centuries, that book would be translated into Latin and studied across Europe, shaping ideas about vision, lenses and the scientific method itself. Yusuf became one of the finest copyists in Cairo, and he never forgot the lesson of the dark room. Today, every time someone takes a photograph, a little light passes through a little hole, just as it once did in a shuttered room in Cairo.

pages.text: For almost two years, Yusuf had been recording the weather from the balcony of his family's flat in Jeddah. Every morning before school, he noted the temperature, the wind direction and the reading on the old brass barometer his grandfather had given him. His classmates had nicknamed him 'the Weatherman', and not always kindly. Yusuf didn't mind, though. To him, the sky was like a book written in a language that only a few people bothered to learn.

That winter, the whole family set off for a camping trip in a wadi in the mountains east of the city. Uncle Khalid, who prided himself on being an experienced camper, chose a spot right in the middle of the dry riverbed, where the sand was soft and flat. 'Perfect,' he announced, hammering in the first tent peg. Above them, the sky was a flawless, cloudless blue. Yet when Yusuf checked the small barometer he had packed, he noticed that the pressure had been falling steadily since the morning.

By mid-afternoon, a line of dark clouds had gathered over the distant peaks, their tops spreading out like enormous anvils. Every so often, Yusuf caught a faint rumble of thunder, so quiet it could almost have been his imagination. 'It's miles away,' said his sister Maha, without even looking up from her book. 'Relax.' But Yusuf remembered something he had read: rain falling on mountains can rush down dry valleys and cause a flash flood dozens of kilometres away, even under a clear sky.

He found Uncle Khalid lighting the barbecue and explained his concerns as calmly as he could. His uncle burst out laughing. 'Not a single drop has fallen here, Yusuf! You've been reading too many books.' Yusuf felt his face burn, but he refused to back down. He opened his notebook and showed the figures, pointing out how quickly the pressure had dropped. Across the camp, his grandfather had put down his cup of coffee and was listening carefully.

'When I was a young man,' his grandfather said slowly, 'I watched a wadi like this one turn into a river in less than ten minutes. A whole herd of camels was swept away.' He looked up at the mountains for a long moment. 'The desert keeps its secrets well, but the boy is right to be cautious.' He suggested moving the tents to a rocky ledge higher up the valley side. Uncle Khalid grumbled that it was a waste of time, but eventually he agreed, muttering that he was doing it against his better judgement.

After the Maghrib prayer, the family carried everything up the slope in the fading light. Uncle Khalid complained loudly the whole way, especially when he had to drag the heavy barbecue over the rocks. Once the new camp had been set up, the night grew strangely still. Then a cool breeze drifted down from the mountains, carrying the rich smell of wet earth. Yusuf frowned, because there still wasn't a cloud above them.

At around ten o'clock, a low roar began to echo through the valley, growing louder by the second, like an approaching train. Everyone scrambled to their feet. Uncle Khalid switched on his torch and pointed the beam down into the wadi. A wall of brown, foaming water was surging through the riverbed, tearing up bushes and carrying broken branches along with it. It was pouring straight over the place where their tents had stood only a few hours earlier.

For a long time, nobody said a word as they watched the water race past below them. Uncle Khalid's face had turned pale in the torchlight. 'If we had stayed down there…' he began, but he couldn't bring himself to finish the sentence. Finally, he put a heavy hand on Yusuf's shoulder. 'I owe you an apology,' he said quietly. 'I should have listened to you instead of laughing.'

By morning, the flood had disappeared as suddenly as it had arrived, leaving behind a wadi floor of thick mud and flattened plants. Back at school, his classmates still called Yusuf 'the Weatherman', but somehow it now sounded more like a compliment than a joke. A week later, Uncle Khalid turned up with a brand-new digital weather station and a card. On it, in his untidy handwriting, were the words: 'For the person who knows when to speak up — and for the rest of us, who are learning when to listen.' Yusuf mounted it on the balcony that very afternoon, right beside his grandfather's old brass barometer.

pages.text: Every summer, Lina left the heat of Riyadh behind and stayed with her grandmother in the cool mountains near Abha. This year, however, the visit came with bad news. Her uncle Fahad had decided to renovate the family's old stone house, and the workers were due on Thursday to cover the walls of the majlis with fresh white paint. Those walls were covered in Al-Qatt Al-Asiri, the bright geometric patterns that women in the region had painted for centuries. 'It's a shame,' Uncle Fahad admitted, 'but the paint is cracking, and nobody has the time or the money to restore it.'

On Tuesday afternoon, Lina sat alone in the majlis, determined to remember every line before it disappeared. She had been sketching for nearly an hour when she noticed something strange. In each long band of red triangles, there was exactly one green triangle, as if the painter had made a careless mistake. Yet the mistake appeared again and again, always in the same position. 'Teta,' she called, 'why would anyone get the same thing wrong so many times?'

Her grandmother lowered herself onto a cushion and smiled at the wall as though greeting an old friend. 'My mother, Sharifa, painted this room before I was born,' she explained. 'She always left one broken triangle, because she believed that only Allah makes things perfect.' She paused, her eyes shining. 'That green triangle was her signature. Anyone who knew her work would have recognised it immediately.'

That evening, Lina received a message from her art teacher, Ms. Nora, with a link to a news article. A regional museum in Abha was about to open an exhibition of traditional wall paintings, and its most important piece was a panel that had been removed from a village house decades earlier. According to the article, the artist was unknown. Lina zoomed in on the photograph, and her heart almost stopped. There, in the third row of red triangles, sat a single green one.

'You've been reading too many detective novels,' Uncle Fahad laughed when she showed him her phone. 'Hundreds of women used similar designs, so it could easily be a coincidence.' Lina refused to give up, but she knew a photograph alone wouldn't convince anyone. Then her grandmother disappeared into her bedroom and returned with a small wooden box. Inside lay a faded notebook, its pages filled with careful drawings of patterns, colours and measurements.

The next morning, Lina, her grandmother and her cousin Yousef were waiting outside the museum before it had even opened. The curator, Dr. Amal, listened politely at first, clearly expecting another family story with no evidence behind it. However, when she opened the notebook, her expression changed completely. On page twelve was a sketch of the exact panel in her exhibition, complete with the green triangle and a note in neat handwriting: 'For my neighbour Umm Saleh's house.' Dr. Amal looked up slowly. 'Do you realise what you've found?'

There was no time to celebrate, because it was already Wednesday and the workers would arrive the following day. Dr. Amal insisted on seeing the majlis herself, so they drove back up the winding mountain road as the sun was setting. Standing in the painted room, she ran her fingers gently along the cracked surface. 'If this room is painted over, we'll lose one of the finest examples of Al-Qatt Al-Asiri I've ever seen,' she said. By the time she had finished speaking, Uncle Fahad was already on the phone, cancelling the workers.

Within a month, everything had changed. The label beside the museum panel was replaced with a new one that read: 'Painted by Sharifa bint Ali, mid-twentieth century.' Even better, the museum offered to help restore the family majlis so that visitors could one day see Sharifa's work in its original home. Uncle Fahad, who had once considered the walls a problem, now proudly showed them to anyone who would listen. 'I always said this house was special,' he declared, and nobody had the heart to remind him otherwise.

On the last day of the summer, Lina's grandmother handed her a brush and a small pot of red paint. Together, they began decorating a plain wall in the kitchen, with Teta patiently correcting the angle of every line. Lina worked slowly, concentrating so hard that she barely noticed the afternoon passing. When the final band was nearly complete, she hesitated, then reached for the green paint. Her grandmother watched her paint one small triangle and laughed softly. 'Now,' she said, 'the family has two signatures.'

stories.title: The Roots That Held the Sea

pages.text: Faisal had always assumed that the mangroves on the edge of his village would outlast everyone he knew. His grandfather had planted the first seedlings forty years earlier, wading into the warm Red Sea shallows with a bucket of muddy shoots while his neighbours laughed at him. Now the trees stood taller than a man, their tangled roots arching out of the water like the fingers of a giant hand. So when Faisal noticed wooden stakes tied with bright orange tape running straight through the forest one Friday afternoon, he felt a cold knot form in his stomach.

By Sunday, a huge sign had appeared beside the coast road, showing a glossy picture of yachts, white hotels and a marina where the mangroves should have been. Faisal's grandfather read it slowly, then turned away without saying a word, which worried Faisal far more than any angry speech would have done. That evening, his older sister Lama slammed her laptop shut at the dinner table. "We can't just sit on our hands while they bulldoze Jaddi's life's work," she declared. "If the council has already approved it, there's nothing we can do," their father replied gently, but Lama's eyes were already shining with a plan.

Lama had been studying environmental science at university and had recently been lent a drone for a research project. Together with Mr. Idris, Faisal's science teacher, they decided to gather evidence of everything the mangroves did for the village. Every morning before school, Faisal counted herons and crabs, measured young fish caught in the roots, and recorded the data in a notebook that soon became soaked with sea spray. Still, he couldn't shake off his doubts. "Honestly, who's going to listen to two teenagers and a borrowed drone?" he muttered one day, and Mr. Idris simply smiled and said, "Facts have a way of being heard, eventually."

Two weeks later, the weather service issued an urgent warning: an unusually powerful storm was heading towards the coast. The construction company had already begun clearing a strip of mangroves at the northern end of the bay, leaving nothing but bare, churned-up mud. That night, the wind howled around the house like a wounded animal, and Faisal lay awake listening to the rain hammering against the windows. At around two o'clock, he heard a roar he had never heard before, deeper than thunder, and realised with horror that it was the sea itself.

At first light, Lama launched the drone, and the two of them watched the screen in stunned silence. Where the trees had been cut down, the waves had surged inland, swallowing the coast road and flooding a row of houses up to their windows. Yet behind the untouched mangroves, barely a kilometre away, the homes stood completely dry, protected by that dense wall of roots. "Are you recording this?" Faisal whispered, hardly daring to breathe. "Every single second," Lama replied, her voice trembling.

The municipal council held a public meeting the following week, and to Faisal's dismay, Lama insisted that he should present their findings. Standing before a room full of serious officials, his hands shook so badly that his notes rattled like dry leaves. A smartly dressed representative from the construction company listened politely, then dismissed the data as "charming, but hardly scientific." "With respect," he added, "a few crabs cannot stand in the way of progress." Faisal felt his cheeks burn, and for a terrible moment he wished the floor would open up and swallow him.

Then his grandfather rose slowly from the back row, leaning on his walking stick. "Forty years ago, I planted those trees because the old fishermen told me the sea would one day grow hungry," he said quietly. "Last week, it did, and it ate only where the trees were gone." At that moment, Lama nodded to Mr. Idris, who pressed play, and the drone footage filled the screen: the flooded road on one side, the dry, peaceful houses on the other. Nobody spoke, and even the company representative stared at the floor.

After a long discussion, the council voted to suspend the project until a full environmental assessment had been carried out. Within three months, the plans had been completely redesigned, with the marina moved to an area of empty land further south. Even more surprisingly, the construction company agreed to fund the replanting of the cleared strip, having realised that a protected coastline would make their hotels far safer. A national newspaper ran a story about the village, and Faisal's slightly blurry photo of a heron appeared on the front page.

On a calm spring morning, Faisal waded into the shallows beside his grandfather, a bucket of muddy seedlings in his hands. "Your neighbours laughed at you once," he said, pressing a young shoot firmly into the mud. "Let them laugh," his grandfather chuckled. "Trees are patient, and they always have the last word." Faisal looked out at the silver water and realised that, one day, he would be the one telling this story to someone younger, standing beneath trees he had planted himself.

pages.text: Layla had been at Al-Yasmin Girls' School for exactly three weeks, and she still ate lunch alone. Back in Dammam she had been surrounded by friends who knew her jokes before she finished telling them. Here in Riyadh, the other girls were polite but distant, as if she were a guest who had overstayed her welcome. The only place she felt at ease was the school library, a quiet room that smelled of old paper and cardamom from the librarian's flask. It was there, on a dull Tuesday afternoon, that she found the first note.

It was tucked between pages 88 and 89 of a worn adventure novel, folded into a neat square. In careful blue handwriting, it said: "To whoever is reading this: the hardest chapters are usually in the middle. Keep going." Layla read it three times, her heart beating strangely fast. It could have been meant for anyone, of course, yet it felt as though it had been written especially for her. She slipped it into her pencil case and, for the first time in weeks, smiled all the way home.

Over the next fortnight, Layla turned into something of a detective. She borrowed book after book, and every few days another note appeared, always in the same blue ink. "Someone is glad you exist," one read. Another said, "Being new is temporary. Being you is permanent." Finding the writer, however, was like looking for a needle in a haystack, since hundreds of girls used the library every week.

Her prime suspect was Mrs Haifa, the librarian, who greeted every student as though she were a long-lost niece. But when Layla casually compared the notes with a handwritten library poster, the letters looked nothing alike. Next she suspected Reem, a cheerful girl from the year above who was always organising charity events. Unfortunately, Reem's handwriting turned out to be a messy scrawl that nobody could have mistaken for those elegant blue loops. Layla was running out of ideas, and she was beginning to wonder whether she would ever solve the mystery.

Then, one Thursday, she decided to stay behind after the final bell and keep watch from behind a tall shelf of encyclopaedias. For forty minutes nothing happened apart from the slow ticking of the clock and the hum of the air conditioner. Just as she was about to give up, the door creaked open. A girl walked in, glanced around nervously, and pulled a folded square of paper from her abaya pocket. Layla held her breath, because she recognised her immediately: it was Noura, the girl everyone in class called "the Ice Queen."

Noura hardly ever spoke, rarely smiled, and sat at the back of the room with her headphones around her neck like a shield. Layla had assumed, like everyone else, that she simply thought she was better than the rest of them. Now she watched Noura slide the note carefully into a book, then hesitate, as if she might take it back. Layla stepped out from behind the shelf before she could stop herself. "So it's you," she said softly. Noura jumped so violently that she nearly dropped the whole pile of books she was carrying.

For a moment, Noura looked as if she wanted the floor to swallow her up. "Please don't tell anyone," she whispered, her cheeks burning. "Two years ago, when my family moved here from Tabuk, I barely spoke to anyone for months." She explained that she had a stammer which got worse whenever she was anxious, so talking to new people felt like climbing a mountain. "Then someone left a note in a library book for me, and it got me through the worst term of my life, so I promised myself I'd pass it on."

Layla felt a wave of shame wash over her as she remembered how quickly she had judged Noura by her cover. She reached into her pencil case and took out every note she had collected, smoothing them flat on the table. "These kept me going too," she admitted. "You've been talking to me for weeks; I just didn't know it was you." Noura stared at the little pile of paper, and slowly, unexpectedly, a shy smile spread across her face.

The following Sunday, Layla carried her lunch tray straight past the empty table where she usually sat and stopped beside Noura. "Is this seat taken?" she asked, and Noura shook her head, moving her bag aside. They didn't talk much that day, but the silence felt comfortable rather than lonely. That afternoon, Layla went to the library, chose a book from the bottom shelf, and slipped a note of her own inside it, written in green ink. It said simply: "You are not as alone as you think."
