stories.title: The Night the Lights Went Out

pages.text: Faisal had always thought of the beach below his grandfather's house in Umluj as the most boring place on earth. Every summer his family drove from Riyadh to spend two weeks there, and every summer he counted the days until they could leave. This year, however, something had changed: a new resort had been built at the far end of the bay, and its enormous floodlights now turned the night sky a strange, glowing orange. "It's like living next to a football stadium," his sister Reem complained, pulling the curtains shut. Faisal shrugged, unaware that those lights were about to turn his holiday upside down.

It was almost midnight when he heard his grandfather calling urgently from the terrace. The old man, who had fished these waters for fifty years, was pointing at the sand with a trembling hand. Dozens of tiny dark shapes were scuttling across the beach, but not towards the sea. They were heading inland, straight towards the road. "Hatchlings," Grandfather whispered. "Green turtles. They should be going to the water."

Faisal grabbed his phone to use the torch, but his grandfather stopped him. "No light! That's the whole problem," he said. He explained that baby turtles find the sea by heading towards the brightest horizon, which for millions of years has been moonlight reflecting off the waves. Now the resort's floodlights were brighter than the moon, so the hatchlings were being lured in exactly the wrong direction. If they reached the road, or if the sun rose before they found the water, they would not survive.

Reem was already pulling on her sandals. "Then we carry them," she said, as though it were the most obvious thing in the world. The three of them knelt on the cool sand and began gently scooping up the hatchlings, each no bigger than a date, and placing them in a plastic bucket. Their flippers beat frantically against Faisal's palms, and he was surprised by how determined such small creatures could be. Within half an hour they had rescued forty-three, but more were still emerging from the nest.

"We can't keep doing this all night," Faisal said, wiping sweat from his forehead. "We need to deal with the cause, not just the symptoms." He looked across the bay at the blazing resort and made up his mind. Before his grandfather could object, he was jogging along the shoreline, rehearsing in his head what he would say. By the time he reached the gates, his heart was pounding, and not only from the run.

The night security guard, a tired-looking man called Hassan, listened politely but shook his head. "I'm sorry, but I'd lose my job if I switched off the lights without permission," he said. Faisal's confidence began to crumble, but then he remembered the video on his phone of the hatchlings crawling helplessly towards the road. He held it out without a word. Hassan watched it twice, sighed deeply, and picked up his radio to call the manager.

The manager, Ms Nouf Al-Harbi, arrived ten minutes later, clearly annoyed at being woken up. However, as soon as she had seen the footage, her expression softened. "I had no idea," she admitted. "Nobody told us this beach was a nesting site." She gave the order, and one by one the huge floodlights flickered and died, until only the stars and a thin crescent moon remained.

When Faisal got back, breathless, the beach looked completely different. Silver moonlight was shimmering on the water, and the remaining hatchlings had turned around as if someone had flicked a switch inside them. Reem and Grandfather were emptying the bucket at the water's edge, and the little turtles were scrambling into the foam and disappearing beneath the waves. "You did it," Reem said, and for once she wasn't teasing him. Grandfather simply put a hand on his shoulder, which meant more than any words.

The following week, the resort replaced its floodlights with low amber lamps that faced away from the beach, and Ms Al-Harbi invited Faisal to help design signs warning guests about the nests. Scientists say that only about one hatchling in a thousand survives to adulthood, so Faisal knew their rescue was just a drop in the ocean. Still, he liked to imagine one of those tiny turtles returning to this very beach in twenty-five years to lay her own eggs. On the last night of the holiday, he found himself sitting on the dark sand, in no hurry at all to leave. The most boring place on earth, he realised, had been hiding its magic all along.

pages.text: Layan had been holding her breath for so long that her chest ached when the rocket finally disappeared into the clouds above the launch site. Thousands of kilometres away, in a small laboratory at her school in Riyadh, she and four classmates were watching the live stream with their teacher, Ms. Hessa. Somewhere inside that rocket was Najm, a satellite no bigger than a tissue box, which the girls had spent two years designing, building and testing. Ninety minutes later, as Najm passed over Arabia for the first time, a series of clear, cheerful beeps came through the speakers. The room exploded with cheers, and Ms. Hessa, who rarely showed her emotions, quietly wiped her eyes.

The celebration did not last long. On the next pass, the speakers produced nothing but a soft hiss, and the pass after that was exactly the same. For three days the team took turns at the ground station, staring at a screen that refused to show a single signal. "It happens to professional engineers all the time," Ms. Hessa told them gently, though her voice lacked its usual confidence. "Sometimes a satellite simply goes quiet, and we never find out why."

That evening Layan barely touched her dinner, and her grandfather, who missed nothing, noticed at once. For thirty years he had worked as a radio operator at an airport, guiding pilots through storms with nothing but his voice and a pair of headphones. When she explained what had happened, he stroked his white beard thoughtfully and was silent for a while. "In my experience, the sky is rarely truly silent," he said at last. "More often, we are simply not listening in the right way."

After the family had prayed Isha, he led her up to the roof, carrying an old receiver that had been gathering dust in a cupboard for years. The night air was cool, and above the glow of the city a few brave stars were shining. "Your satellite was built to speak on one frequency," he explained, slowly turning a dial, "but machines, like people, do not always behave as expected." For almost an hour they heard only static, and Layan was beginning to feel foolish. Then, just slightly to one side of where it should have been, a faint, thin whistle rose and fell like a distant bird.

Layan stared at the receiver, hardly daring to believe her ears. Suddenly the pieces fell into place: in the freezing darkness of space, the tiny crystal that controlled Najm's radio must have grown colder than they had predicted, pushing its signal a little off course. Worse still, the strange rhythm of the beeps suggested that the satellite had restarted itself in "safe mode" and was now waiting patiently for instructions. Nobody had answered, of course, because nobody had heard it calling. Although it was nearly midnight, she grabbed her phone and rang Ms. Hessa, who picked up on the first ring.

By three o'clock in the morning, the whole team had gathered in the laboratory, their parents sitting sleepily in the corridor with flasks of Arabic coffee. According to their calculations, Najm would rise above the horizon at 3:47 and remain within reach for just nine minutes. In that short window, they would have to send the command that would wake the satellite fully, using the shifted frequency that her grandfather had found. If they missed this chance, the next suitable pass would not come for another two days, and by then the batteries might have run out. Layan's grandfather sat beside her, his old headphones resting around his neck.

At 3:47 exactly, the faint whistle crept into the speakers, and everyone in the room fell silent. Noor typed in the command and pressed send, but the screen showed no reply. They tried a second time, then a third, while the clock ticked mercilessly towards the moment when Najm would slip below the horizon. "The signal is drifting again," her grandfather murmured, listening with his eyes closed. "It is warming up as it moves into sunlight, so follow it with your ear, not with your numbers." Trusting her instincts, Layan turned the dial a fraction to the left, and Noor sent the command one last time.

For three agonising seconds, nothing happened, and then lines of data began pouring across the screen. The batteries were healthy, the solar panels were working, and every system reported that it was ready. Nobody spoke for a moment, as if they were afraid the satellite might disappear again if they made a sound. Two days later, on a perfectly clear pass, Najm sent down its very first photograph: the Arabian Peninsula at night, its cities scattered like golden jewels across the dark desert. In the middle of it all, unmistakably, shone Riyadh.

The following week, a newspaper ran a story about the schoolgirls who had rescued their satellite against all odds, and Ms. Hessa insisted that the team's mentor should be named as well. Layan printed the photograph and framed it for her grandfather, who hung it proudly above his old receiver. "So you see," he said, smiling, "the sky was talking to you all along." Layan laughed, but she knew she would never forget the lesson. Whether she was listening to a satellite, a classmate or a problem that seemed impossible, she would remember to listen a little more carefully, and slightly to one side.

pages.text: Every summer, Faisal's grandfather took on a new restoration project in Jeddah's historic district of Al-Balad, and this year he had chosen the most neglected house on the street. Its coral-stone walls were crumbling, and its tall wooden mashrabiya, the carved balcony that had once shaded a whole family from the sun, was rotting away piece by piece. Faisal, who was fifteen, had agreed to help on the condition that his cousin Lama could join them, since she was the only person he knew who noticed things nobody else did. "Don't expect anything exciting," his grandfather warned them on the first morning. "Restoration is mostly dust, patience and very sore backs."

On the third morning, Faisal climbed the scaffolding and froze. A panel that had been hanging loose the evening before was now fitted perfectly into the frame, its delicate star pattern restored as if it had never been damaged. He called his grandfather, who examined it for a long time without saying a word. "None of my workers touched this," the old man said finally, running his thumb along the joints. "Whoever did it knows more about this wood than I do."

By the end of the week, three more panels had been mysteriously repaired, and the rumours had spread through the neighbourhood like wildfire. The man who ran the tea stall on the corner insisted that the house was protecting itself, while a neighbour claimed she had heard tapping in the middle of the night. Faisal laughed off the stories, but he had to admit that the whole situation didn't add up. Lama, meanwhile, had been unusually quiet. "Houses don't repair themselves," she said, crouching beside the wall with her phone torch. "People do, and people always leave something behind."

She was right, as it turned out. Beneath the balcony, they found a thin layer of fresh sawdust that smelled sweet and rich, quite unlike the dry, grey dust of the old timber. Their grandfather sniffed it and recognised it immediately as teak, an expensive wood that had to be imported and that his team hadn't used for years. Lama also pointed out a set of footprints in the dust, one foot pressed deeply into the ground and the other barely touching it. "Our carpenter walks with a limp," she concluded, "and he must have been coming here for nights without anyone spotting him."

With their grandfather's permission, the cousins decided to keep watch from the house next door, where an old family friend let them sit by an upstairs window. They had brought dates, a flask of Arabic coffee and enough determination to last until dawn, or so they thought. By two o'clock, Faisal's eyelids were growing heavy and he was beginning to wonder whether the whole idea had been a waste of time. Then Lama gripped his arm so suddenly that he almost knocked the flask over.

A thin figure was making his way slowly along the alley, carrying a cloth bag over one shoulder. He stopped beneath the mashrabiya, glanced around cautiously, and began to climb the scaffolding with surprising skill for someone who moved so stiffly. For almost an hour they watched him work in silence, his hands moving with a confidence that only decades of practice could have given him. When the call to the dawn prayer began to echo across the rooftops, he packed up his tools and disappeared into the shadows before Faisal could even get down the stairs.

Back home, Lama couldn't stop thinking about one detail: before leaving, the stranger had pressed his palm against the wood, almost tenderly, as though greeting an old friend. On a hunch, she asked their grandfather whether he had any photographs of the house from the past. He brought out a faded album, and there, in a picture dated more than fifty years earlier, stood a young man proudly holding a carved panel in front of the brand-new balcony. Their grandfather's eyes widened in disbelief. "That's Hamdan the carpenter," he whispered. "He built this mashrabiya when I was still a boy, and I'd assumed he had passed away long ago."

It took them two days of asking around before they tracked down Uncle Hamdan, who lived alone in a tiny flat above a spice shop. At first he denied everything, but when Lama mentioned the teak sawdust, he sighed and admitted the truth with a tired smile. "I couldn't stand watching my work fall apart," he explained. "I would have offered to help, but I didn't want anyone to think I was a burden, an old man with a bad leg getting in the way." Faisal's grandfather took his hand warmly and told him that the only thing that had been getting in the way was his pride.

From that day on, Uncle Hamdan came to the house every morning, in broad daylight, and he was treated by the whole team as the master he truly was. He insisted on teaching Faisal how to read the grain of the wood and how to join pieces without a single nail, just as his own teacher had taught him. By the end of the summer, the mashrabiya was complete, and the neighbours who had once whispered about a mysterious presence now came to admire it. On the last panel, hidden where only the sharpest eyes would find it, Faisal carved two small letters beside the old craftsman's mark. Lama spotted them at once, of course, but she promised to keep his secret.

pages.text: It was almost midnight, and Yusuf had been staring at the same lines of code for three hours. On the workbench in his family's garage lay Saqr, the small search drone he had spent the whole year building, with one cracked propeller and a navigation system that refused to work. The regional drone competition was in two days, and his partner, Khalid, had dropped out that afternoon to play in a football tournament instead. Yusuf rubbed his eyes and noticed the faded sticker on the side of the drone: H+Y ENGINEERING. Hamad had written it in thick black marker when they were eleven, back when they had still been best friends.

Everything had changed last year in the school cafeteria. Some boys Yusuf had been trying hard to impress had started copying the way Hamad stammered whenever he was nervous. Yusuf had laughed along with them, not because it was funny, but because he desperately wanted to fit in. When he looked up, Hamad was standing behind them with his tray, and the hurt in his eyes had been impossible to miss. Since then, a wall of silence had grown between them, and Yusuf had kept telling himself it would blow over. It never had.

Now Yusuf scrolled through the navigation code and felt his stomach drop. Most of it had been written by Hamad, and the notes between the lines were full of their old private jokes, like "If this fails, blame the camel." Nobody else in the world would be able to understand how it worked. The next morning, after a sleepless night, Yusuf found himself walking to the house on the next street, quietly rehearsing what he would say. When Hamad's younger brother opened the door and shouted his name, Yusuf almost turned around and ran.

Hamad appeared in the doorway with his arms folded. "So you still remember where I live," he said coldly. Yusuf began explaining about the drone, then stopped, realising that this was not the conversation he actually needed to have. "I'm sorry about what happened in the cafeteria," he said at last, forcing himself to swallow his pride. "I didn't laugh because it was funny. I laughed because I was a coward." Hamad was silent for a long moment before he finally stepped aside and muttered, "Show me the code, but I'm doing this for Saqr, not for you."

They worked side by side until late that evening, and slowly the old rhythm returned, almost as if the past year had never happened. Just after ten o'clock, Hamad found the bug: a single line that Yusuf had "improved" months earlier, which had been confusing the drone's sense of direction ever since. "Blame the camel," Yusuf said, and for the first time in a year, they both burst out laughing. Then Yusuf mentioned, as casually as he could, that the competition included a five-minute spoken presentation to the judges. Hamad's smile disappeared, and he reluctantly admitted that he had been practising with a speech therapist, but he wasn't sure he was ready.

On the day of the competition, the university field on the edge of Riyadh was crowded with teams, parents and nervous engineers. The challenge was simple to explain but difficult to complete: each drone had ten minutes to locate a "missing hiker", a dummy hidden somewhere in a marked area of desert. Shortly after Saqr took off, a powerful gust of wind swept across the field, lifting clouds of dust into the air. Two rival drones drifted helplessly off course, and then the screen in front of Yusuf began to flicker. "We're losing the signal!" he shouted, his hands shaking on the controller.

"Falcon's return," Hamad said suddenly. Years earlier, they had programmed a secret manual override that made the drone climb higher and hover until it could reconnect, and they had named it after the way a falcon circles back to its owner. Yusuf hesitated, terrified that it might crash the drone completely, but Hamad looked straight at him and said, "Trust it. We built it together." Yusuf pressed the button, and Saqr rose steadily above the dust until the picture cleared. There, beside a small rocky hill, lay the orange jacket of the dummy, with only forty seconds left on the clock.

In the presentation hall, Yusuf quietly offered to do all the talking, but Hamad shook his head. "We built it together, so we explain it together," he said. Halfway through, Hamad got stuck on a difficult word, and Yusuf noticed one of the boys from the cafeteria smirk in the front row. This time, Yusuf did not laugh; he simply stepped a little closer to his friend and waited calmly, as though they had all the time in the world. Hamad took a deep breath, finished his sentence clearly, and the room filled with warm applause.

Saqr finished in second place, and the judges praised the team for the clever override that had saved their mission. Strangely, neither boy felt disappointed, because they both knew they had won something far more valuable than a trophy. That evening, back in the garage, Yusuf carefully peeled the old, faded sticker off the drone. Hamad grinned, pulled a thick black marker from his pocket and wrote on a fresh label: H+Y ENGINEERING — VERSION TWO. "The first version had a few bugs," he said, "but this one is going to last."

stories.title: The Stone That Fell from the Sky

pages.text: For most of his fifteen years, Fahad had thought of the Empty Quarter as nothing more than a huge blank space on the map of Arabia. So when his Uncle Majed, a geologist, invited him on a three-day expedition to the Wabar craters, he could hardly believe his luck. According to his uncle, a meteorite had crashed into the sand there hundreds of years ago, scattering fragments of iron across the dunes. "If we're lucky, we might find a piece that nobody has touched since it fell," Uncle Majed said, his eyes shining. Fahad packed his bag that night, although he was far too excited to sleep.

They set off before dawn, the four-wheel-drive car humming along a rough track until even the track gave up and disappeared. All around them, dunes rose like frozen waves, shifting from pale gold to deep orange as the sun climbed higher. Uncle Majed explained that the impact had been so violent that it had melted the sand into black glass, which local people had once called "desert pearls." Fahad listened, but part of his mind drifted back to his grandfather, who had spent his youth crossing these sands with camels. "The desert takes away every road," the old man liked to say, "but it can never take away the stars."

By midday they had reached the craters, wide hollows half buried by centuries of drifting sand. They spent hours walking slowly across the ground, heads bent, examining every dark shape they came across. Fahad picked up a heavy, rust-coloured stone and held it out hopefully, but his uncle only glanced at it and shrugged. "Probably just an ordinary rock, but keep it if you like," he said kindly. Fahad slipped it into his pocket anyway, feeling a little foolish. Then, late in the afternoon, he noticed that the horizon had turned a strange, dirty yellow.

"Sandstorm," Uncle Majed muttered. "Get in the car, quickly!" Within minutes the wind was howling like an angry animal, and the world outside the windows vanished into a whirling cloud of dust. They sat in silence for nearly two hours while sand hissed against the metal and the car rocked from side to side. When the storm finally died down, the landscape looked completely unfamiliar, and their tyre tracks had been wiped away as if they had never existed. Worse still, the GPS screen had gone blank, and the satellite phone, which had been charging from the faulty socket, was completely dead.

As if things weren't bad enough, Uncle Majed twisted his ankle while climbing a dune to look around. He limped back to the car, his face tight with pain, and admitted that the wheels had sunk deep into the soft sand. "We should have been more careful," he sighed. "Nobody is expecting us back for two more days." Fahad felt panic rising in his chest, but he forced himself to breathe slowly. If they waited for rescue, they might run out of water; if they drove in the wrong direction, they could end up even more lost.

That was when Fahad remembered the patrol road his uncle had pointed out on the paper map, running roughly north of the craters. "If I can find north, we can find the road," he said, surprising himself with how calm he sounded. First, following his uncle's instructions, he let some air out of the tyres and dug the sand away from the wheels until his hands were raw. Because his uncle's left ankle was injured and the car was automatic, Uncle Majed could still drive with his right foot. Then, as darkness fell and the sky filled with countless stars, Fahad searched for the shape his grandfather had taught him to recognise. There it was: the faint, steady light of the North Star, which never moves while the other stars turn around it.

They drove at a snail's pace through the night, with Fahad leaning out of the window to keep the star directly ahead of them. Every few minutes doubt crept in, and he wondered whether he had made a terrible mistake. "Are you sure about this?" he asked once, his voice shaking slightly. "I trust you more than I trust that broken screen," his uncle replied, and the words gave Fahad the courage to keep going. Hours passed, and the stars wheeled slowly overhead, but the North Star held its position, just as his grandfather had promised.

Just as the sky began to lighten before dawn, the car's headlights caught something straight and solid among the dunes. It was the patrol road, exactly where Fahad had hoped it would be. They stopped to pray, and soon afterwards a Bedouin herder appeared with his camels, as if the desert itself had sent him. He welcomed them warmly, offering sweet tea and dates, and used his own phone to call for help. When Fahad explained how they had found the road, the old herder nodded with approval. "Your grandfather taught you well," he said. "Few young people today can read the sky."

A week later, back in Riyadh, Uncle Majed phoned with news that left Fahad speechless. Almost as an afterthought, he had taken the rust-coloured stone to the university laboratory, and the tests had revealed that it was genuine meteoritic iron. "It seems I owe you an apology, and probably a place in my next research paper," his uncle laughed. That evening, Fahad placed the stone in his grandfather's wrinkled hand and told him the whole story. The old man turned it over slowly, then smiled. "So the sky gave you two gifts," he said, "a stone to hold, and the stars to guide you home."

pages.text: It was 11:47 on a Thursday night when Faisal made the biggest mistake of his fifteen years. He had been chatting with his best friend, Majed, about the family gathering at his grandparents' house the next day. "Honestly," he said into his phone, holding down the record button, "if Aunt Huda brings that date cake again, I'm going to fake an illness. Last time I nearly broke a tooth, and I'm telling you, it's not a cake, it's a building material." He let go of the button, sent the message, and only then noticed the name at the top of the screen: "The Family 🌴 (43 members)".

For three long seconds, Faisal simply stared, unable to breathe. Then he jabbed at the screen, desperate to delete the message for everyone. At that exact moment, his phone, which he had been meaning to charge for two hours, gave a tiny, sad buzz and went completely black. By the time he had found his charger under a pile of school books and switched the phone back on, the app kept freezing, and the delete option had mysteriously vanished. Nobody had listened to the message yet, but in a few hours forty-three people would wake up.

In a panic, he woke his older sister, Noura, who listened to his explanation with her eyes half-closed. "So let me get this straight," she said slowly. "You called Aunt Huda's cake a building material, in front of the entire family, including Aunt Huda." "In front of their phones," Faisal corrected her. "That's completely different, because if I can stop them from playing it, nobody ever has to know." Noura yawned and told him that the whole plan was a recipe for disaster, which, under the circumstances, was an unfortunate choice of words.

Fortunately, Faisal's relatives were famous for two things: arriving late and ignoring the family group, except to send pictures of roses every Friday morning. If he got to his grandparents' house early enough, he might be able to intercept every phone before anyone pressed play. He called it Operation Silent Phone, and he spent the rest of the night planning it as carefully as a bank robbery. By the time the sun came up, he had drawn a map of the house, made a list of every relative, and barely slept at all.

At first, the operation went better than he could have dreamed. He offered to update Uncle Saad's phone "for security reasons" and quietly hid the family chat in a folder his uncle would never find. He convinced his twin cousins that Grandfather wanted a phone-free gathering, and they handed over their phones without a single question. Grandmother, whose phone always rang at full volume, happily let him take hers to the kitchen to charge, where it ended up, for reasons he couldn't fully explain, inside an empty rice container. By lunchtime, Faisal was feeling like a secret agent who deserved a medal.

Then, just as everyone was sitting down with their tea, Grandfather cleared his throat and made an announcement. "I have learned something new," he said proudly, holding up his ancient phone, which nobody had even remembered he owned. "Little Abdullah taught me how to listen to these voice messages, so let us hear what the family has been saying." Faisal leapt forward, but he tripped over a cushion, and before he could get up, Grandfather had pressed the newest message with the speaker turned all the way up.

Faisal's voice filled the room, loud and clear: "It's not a cake, it's a building material." The silence that followed was the longest of his life, and he would have given anything for the floor to swallow him whole. Aunt Huda slowly put down her cup, and every head turned towards her, then towards Faisal, who was still lying on the carpet next to the cushion. Somewhere in the kitchen, as if to make things worse, Grandmother's phone began ringing loudly from inside the rice container.

Then, to everyone's astonishment, Aunt Huda burst out laughing so hard that tears ran down her face. "Twelve years!" she cried. "For twelve years I have baked that awful cake because your grandmother said it was everybody's favourite, and every single one of you kept telling me it was delicious!" One by one, the relatives confessed: Uncle Saad admitted he had been hiding his piece in a napkin, and Grandfather admitted he had been feeding his to the birds in the garden. Even Grandmother, who had suggested the recipe in the first place, confessed that she had never actually tasted it.

"Well," said Aunt Huda, wiping her eyes, "since our young expert has such strong opinions, next Friday he can do the baking." A week later, Faisal proudly carried in his own cake, which had collapsed in the middle and burned around the edges. The family ate it politely, without saying a word, until Faisal's phone buzzed with a new voice note in the family group. It was from Aunt Huda, and it said: "Honestly, it's not a cake, it's a pancake that has given up on life." This time, Faisal laughed louder than anyone.

pages.text: Yousef had spent every afternoon that summer at the marine research station on the Farasan Islands, where his uncle Khalid worked as a biologist. His favourite job was watching a small green dot on a computer screen. The dot was Noor, a young hawksbill turtle who had been fitted with a satellite transmitter three weeks earlier. Every six hours, the dot jumped to a new place as Noor wandered between the reefs of the Red Sea. But on Thursday morning, when Yousef refreshed the map, the dot had not moved at all.

"It's probably just a technical fault," Uncle Khalid said, although he was frowning at the screen. "Transmitters fail more often than people realise." Yousef wasn't convinced, and he could tell his uncle wasn't either. If a turtle stays in one spot for too long, it might be resting, but it might also be trapped. The last signal had come from a reef twelve kilometres north, and by now Noor could be anywhere.

Their grandfather, who had been a fisherman for over forty years, was drinking tea by the window and had overheard everything. "The sea doesn't keep things where you leave them," he said calmly. "The wind has been blowing from the north-west for two days, so the current will have pushed anything floating towards the shallows near the Two Sisters." Uncle Khalid explained that the station's boat was being repaired and wouldn't be ready until the following week. Grandfather simply stood up and reached for his keys. "Then we'll take mine," he said, as if the matter had already been decided.

Grandfather's boat was old and noisy, but it cut through the water with surprising confidence. As they headed north, Yousef began to feel that they were looking for a needle in a haystack, because the sea seemed endless and every wave looked the same. Grandfather, however, kept pointing out details that Yousef would never have noticed: a line of foam where two currents met, a change in the colour of the water, a group of seabirds circling low. "The sea talks all the time," he said. "Most people just haven't learned to listen."

They had been searching for almost two hours when Yousef spotted something dark moving near the surface. As they came closer, his stomach turned. A huge abandoned fishing net, heavy with seaweed and plastic, had drifted into the shallows, and caught inside it was a turtle. One of her front flippers was tightly wrapped in the green ropes, and she was struggling to lift her head to breathe. On her shell, Yousef could just make out the small white device that his uncle had attached.

"We're racing against the clock," Uncle Khalid said, pulling on his mask. "She's exhausted, and if she can't reach the surface, she'll drown." Yousef put on his life jacket and slid into the warm water beside him, while Grandfather held the boat steady against the rising waves. Every time the knife came near, Noor panicked and twisted, pulling the ropes even tighter. Yousef held her shell as gently as he could and spoke to her quietly, although he knew she couldn't understand a word.

At last, the final rope snapped and the net fell away into the blue. Noor floated free, but her flipper was badly cut and she barely moved. "If we release her now, she might not survive," Uncle Khalid said, breathing hard. Together, the three of them lifted her carefully into the boat and wrapped her in a wet towel to keep her cool. Then they did something just as important: they hauled the rest of the net on board so that it could never trap another animal.

Back at the station, the vet examined Noor and said that, with a few weeks of rest, she would recover completely. The transmitter, it turned out, had been crushed by the ropes, which explained why the dot had frozen on the screen. "So the technology told us something was wrong," Yousef said slowly, "but it couldn't tell us where to look." Uncle Khalid smiled and glanced at Grandfather. "Satellites are useful," he admitted, "but they've never spent forty years on the water."

Three weeks later, the whole family gathered on the beach at sunrise to watch Noor return to the sea with a brand-new transmitter. She paused at the edge of the water for a moment, then disappeared beneath the waves without looking back. That evening, a fresh green dot appeared on the screen, moving steadily south. Yousef, meanwhile, had started a new project: a notebook filled with everything his grandfather knew about winds, currents and birds. "One day," he said, "someone will need this knowledge, and I don't want it to be lost."

The transmitter had been crushed by the ropes.
The station's computer had broken down.

options: He used the wind direction and his knowledge of currents.
He followed the last satellite signal exactly.
Other fishermen had told him where the net was.

stories.title: The Other Half of the Coin

pages.text: Nora had never thought of herself as an adventurer, so when her father announced that the family would be spending the winter holiday in Uzbekistan, she simply shrugged. That changed the night before they left, when her grandmother called her into her room and placed a faded envelope and half of an old silver coin in her hands. "In 1958, your great-grandfather Abdullah fell seriously ill in Bukhara on his way home from a trading journey," she explained quietly. "A family there looked after him for weeks, and before he left, he broke this coin in two and gave them the other half." She held Nora's gaze. "He always dreamed that someone from our family would go back and thank them properly, and I think that someone should be you."

Two days later, the high-speed train was racing across the frozen plains between Tashkent and Bukhara, while Nora studied the envelope for the hundredth time. The address had been written in an elegant but old-fashioned hand, and according to her phone, half the street names in the city had been changed since then. "Let's be realistic," said her older brother Saud, without looking up from his game. "You're looking for a family you've never met, at an address that probably doesn't exist, from a story that's nearly seventy years old." He grinned. "It's like searching for a needle in a haystack, except someone has moved the haystack."

Unfortunately, Saud turned out to be partly right. When they finally found the spot where the house should have stood, they discovered a smart modern hotel with glass doors and a doorman in a long coat. Nora felt her heart sink, and for a moment she could hardly bring herself to speak. "We've done our best, habibti," her father said gently, resting a hand on her shoulder. "Perhaps we should just enjoy the rest of our trip." However, Nora had made a promise, and she was determined not to give up at the first obstacle.

On the spur of the moment, she marched into the hotel and showed the receptionist a photo of the envelope. The young man frowned at the name for a long time before admitting that he had never heard of the family. "But if anyone knows the history of this city, it's Madina Opa," he added, brightening. "She runs the old bookshop near the Lyabi-Hauz pond, and people say she remembers every story that has ever been told in Bukhara." Nora thanked him so many times that he began to laugh.

The bookshop was tiny and smelled of dust, paper and cardamom tea, and Madina Opa was even tinier, peering at them over a pair of enormous reading glasses. As she examined the envelope, her expression slowly shifted from polite curiosity to astonishment. "My father used to tell this story when I was a girl," she murmured. "A traveller from Arabia who nearly died of fever, and a family of coppersmiths who refused to let him go until he was strong again." She pointed a thin finger towards the window. "If they are still anywhere, they will be in the coppersmiths' quarter, beneath the old trading domes."

By the time Nora and her mother reached the trading domes, the winter sun was already sinking and the air was ringing with the sound of hammers on metal. They went from workshop to workshop, asking the same question again and again, but each craftsman only shook his head apologetically. One by one, the shutters began to come down, and the narrow lanes grew colder and quieter. Nora could feel her hopes fading with the light, and she was beginning to wonder whether she had been foolish to come so far for a story. "One more," her mother insisted, squeezing her hand. "Just one more, and then we'll go."

The last workshop belonged to an elderly man with a white beard, who was polishing a copper tray so carefully that he barely noticed them enter. Nora began to explain, but then she realised he wasn't listening to her words at all; his eyes were fixed on the half-coin in her open palm. Without a word, he put down his cloth and disappeared into the back of the shop. They could hear drawers being opened and boxes being moved, and Nora held her breath. When the old man returned, his hands were trembling, and he was carrying a small wooden box decorated with faded blue paint.

Inside the box, wrapped in a piece of embroidered silk, lay the other half of the coin. When Nora placed the two pieces side by side, they fitted together perfectly, as if they had never been apart. The old man, whose name was Rustam, explained through his grandson that his own grandfather had kept the coin all his life. "He made me promise that I would never sell it, however difficult things became," Rustam said, his voice thick with emotion. "He always said, 'One day, they will come back, and we must be ready to welcome them as family.'" Nora's mother read the letter aloud, translating each line, and by the end, nobody in the workshop had dry eyes.

That evening, Rustam's family insisted on inviting them home for a feast of steaming plov, fresh bread and endless cups of green tea. Nora video-called her grandmother, who wept with joy as Rustam held up his half of the coin to the screen. Before they left, the two families made a decision: rather than joining the coin together, each would keep its half, so that one day another generation would have a reason to make the journey. On the train home, Saud admitted that he had been completely wrong about the haystack. Nora simply smiled and looked out at the snowy plains, realising that the best journeys aren't about the places you see, but about the people who are waiting at the end of them.

options: To thank them for looking after him when he was ill
To pay for a copper tray he had bought
To exchange it for a train ticket home

Who told Nora to look in the coppersmiths' quarter?
